note: Draft texts (task A3). Task A7 rewrites them after checking the real SPHEREx images.
saturated_badge: Saturated center: the camera got more light than it can count, so the brightest pixels are painted with the top color. Look at the edge of the star instead.

targets.name: Barnard's Star
targets.headline: The fastest-moving star in our sky
targets.what_it_is: A small red star only 6 light-years away, one of the Sun's closest neighbors. It crosses the sky faster than any other star: in about 170 years it moves the width of the full Moon.
targets.what_to_look_at: Between August 2025 and September 2026 it moved about 1.7 pixels north (up). In the difference image it leaves a dark spot where it was and a bright spot where it went.

how_to_look.text: Detector 5 or 6, where its saturated center is smallest; difference of season 3 minus season 1. SPHEREx measured 1.70 pixels a year; catalogs say 1.69.

watch_out: It is so bright that its center is saturated in every detector: the camera got more light than it can count. Those pixels are painted with the brightest color.
Charts from 2000 put it a sixth of the Moon's width from where it is today.

targets.name: Epsilon Indi B
targets.headline: Two failed stars with methane in their air
targets.what_it_is: Two brown dwarfs orbiting each other, and together orbiting the star Epsilon Indi A, 12 light-years away. Brown dwarfs are too small to burn like the Sun: they glow in the infrared as they slowly cool.
targets.what_to_look_at: Compare detector 4 with detector 5. Methane in their air absorbs light inside detector 4, so the pair should look dimmer there than in detector 5. That dip is the fingerprint of methane in their spectrum.

how_to_look.text: Use the image of all seasons and switch between detector 4 and detector 5.

watch_out: Epsilon Indi A, a much brighter star, is in the same field. The brown dwarfs are the faint dot at the center.
They move too: about 1.1 pixels south-east (down and to the left) between the first and the last season. SPHEREx measured 0.74 pixels a year; catalogs say 0.75.

targets.name: WISE 0855-0714
targets.headline: The coldest brown dwarf known
targets.what_it_is: A brown dwarf only 7 light-years away, colder than any other found so far. It is so cold that it gives off almost no visible light: it only shines in the longest infrared colors.
targets.what_to_look_at: Open detector 6 with every season added: the faint dot at the center, right where WISE puts it. It moved about 1.3 pixels west (to the right) over the year, a shift too small to follow season by season.

how_to_look.text: Detector 6 only: in detector 5 it is too faint for these images, and it does not show in detectors 1 to 4.

watch_out: A background star sits next to its path: 1.9 pixels away in May 2025, 0.8 in May 2026. In detectors 1 to 4, the dot at the center is that star, not WISE 0855.
The challenge's position is from about 2010; this site centers on where it is today.

targets.name: RW Aurigae
targets.headline: A young star that dims without warning
targets.what_it_is: A very young star, still surrounded by the disk of gas and dust it formed from. Clumps of that dust sometimes pass in front of it and dim it for weeks or months.
targets.what_to_look_at: It does not move. Keep the same detector and step through the 3 seasons: its brightness can change from one season to the next. Measured: in detector 1 it was 1.5 times as bright in September 2026 as in September 2025.

how_to_look.text: Detector 1 (it saturates the least), one season at a time.

watch_out: It is so bright that its center is always saturated in detectors 2, 4, 5 and 6, and sometimes in detectors 1 and 3: the camera got more light than it can count. Those pixels are painted with the brightest color.
Compare the size of its glow rather than its center: a brighter star looks bigger.

targets.name: R Draconis
targets.headline: A giant star that swells and fades every 8 months
targets.what_it_is: An old red giant that pulsates: it grows and shrinks, and its brightness changes a lot, in a cycle of about 247 days. Stars like this are called Mira variables.
targets.what_to_look_at: Keep one detector and step through the 4 seasons. They fall at different points of its cycle, so it should look brighter in some seasons than in others. Measured with SPHEREx alone: it brightens and fades every 244 days or so; catalogs say 247.

how_to_look.text: Any detector, one season at a time.

watch_out: It is so bright that its center is saturated in every detector: the camera got more light than it can count. Those pixels are painted with the brightest color.
It sits near the spot SPHEREx passes over most often, so it has 1259 frames, far more than the others.

detectors.text: Near-infrared just past red light. Stars like the Sun are bright here.
Near-infrared. Dust hides less here than in visible light.
Near-infrared. Cool red stars are brightest around here.
Infrared. Methane gas absorbs light near 3.3 micrometers, inside this band, so methane-rich brown dwarfs look dimmer here.
Longer infrared. Cold brown dwarfs give off most of their light around here.
The longest infrared SPHEREx sees. The coldest objects stand out most.

modes.name: One season
modes.text: The frames of one season in one detector, added together so faint things show up.

modes.name: Difference
modes.text: A later season minus an earlier one. What did not change disappears. A star that moved leaves a dark spot where it was and a bright spot where it went.

modes.name: All seasons
modes.text: Every season added together: the deepest image, but anything that moves looks stretched.

modes.name: All detectors
modes.text: The 6 detectors added together for one season: the most light, without color.

modes.name: Color
modes.text: Detectors 1, 3 and 6 shown as blue, green and red.

layers.name: Gaia
layers.text: Stars measured by ESA's Gaia space telescope, moved to the date of each season.

layers.name: CatWISE
layers.text: Infrared sources seen by NASA's WISE telescope, moved by their measured motion. Entries along the target's own path are hidden: there the catalog is unreliable.

layers.name: SIMBAD
layers.text: Named objects from the SIMBAD database, including the target itself at each season.

layers.name: Asteroids
layers.text: Known asteroids that crossed the field during a visit, only those bright enough for SPHEREx.

flags.name: TRANSIENT
flags.text: Something hit or changed this pixel during the exposure, such as a cosmic ray.

flags.name: OVERFLOW
flags.text: The pixel got more light than it can count: it is saturated and its value is not real. The site paints it with the brightest color.

flags.name: SUR_ERROR
flags.text: The camera could not measure a clean brightness for this pixel during the exposure.

flags.name: NONFUNC
flags.text: A pixel that does not work.

flags.name: DICHROIC
flags.text: Possible stray light from the part of the telescope that splits the light between detectors.

flags.name: MISSING_DATA
flags.text: There is no data for this pixel.

flags.name: HOT
flags.text: A pixel that reads too high even without light.

flags.name: COLD
flags.text: A pixel that is less sensitive than the others.

flags.name: FULLSAMPLE
flags.text: A processing note about how this pixel was read. Not a problem by itself.

flags.name: PHANMISS
flags.text: A correction for an electronic echo of bright stars could not be applied here.

flags.name: NONLINEAR
flags.text: The pixel was nearly full, so its brightness is not reliable. Treated like a saturated pixel.

flags.name: PERSIST
flags.text: Afterglow: a bright source seen earlier may leave a faint trace here.

flags.name: OUTLIER
flags.text: This value disagrees strongly with the other readings of the same spot.

flags.name: CROSSTALK
flags.text: A bright star elsewhere on the detector leaks a faint electronic copy here.

flags.name: SOURCE
flags.text: A star or galaxy covers this pixel. This is normal and never hidden.

flags.name: GHOST
flags.text: A faint reflection of a bright star inside the telescope may fall here.

flags.name: GHOST_FPA
flags.text: A reflection between the detectors and the telescope optics may fall here.

flags.name: GHOST_EXT
flags.text: A reflection of a bright star outside the image may fall here.

flags.name: STREAK
flags.text: A streak crosses this pixel, for example from a satellite.

flags.name: BLOOM
flags.text: Charge spilled over from a saturated neighbor. It is still light from that bright star.

flags.name: SNOWBALL
flags.text: A round splash left by a particle hitting the detector.

flags.name: HALO
flags.text: Inside the glow around a very bright star.

sources.period_days: SIMBAD mesVar, Gaia DR3 long-period variables (2022yCat.1358)
